title: The Meal Chant
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer's talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating generosity, love, and wisdom through simple yet profound acts like eating oryoki meals together as a community. By honoring Buddha and the Bodhisattvas with intention and mindfulness, participants can transform their daily activities into sources of spiritual growth and compassion. This practice is meant to inspire individuals to embody the ideal human life, where they are born into the world with suffering, awaken, teach, and enter nirvana, recognizing the interconnectedness and emptiness of all things.

sentences.text: Well, can you all hear okay?
Before I say anything, I just want to first off remember Nancy, dear Nancy Welch.
Nancy, along with John Wiley (John's still here, right?), were our first lay Zen teachers in the Pacific Northwest.

A dear, dear heart and soul of the Red Cedar Zen community, she died this winter after a long life of nothing but difficult health challenges that she managed, over and over and over again, to overcome with a great spirit.
I know many of you here knew and loved Nancy well.
She was absolutely irrepressible.
Nothing could stop her.
A wise and courageous lady who, despite her terrible rheumatoid arthritis and unbelievable pain, sat numerous sesshins in this room with us.
And she is still sitting with us.
Every time we sit here at Samish, Nancy is going to be here, for sure.
Sometimes you'll be walking down the path, you'll see her.
So I wanted to start with remembering dear Nancy.
Second, I want to thank Tim and Chris for their talks.
You all have been enjoying for a long time this ability to come to the Zendo and hear a good, encouraging Dharma talk.
It's a little new for me.
I like it.
I like it.
And it reminds me of a Japanese poem.
I forget whose, I think it's some haiku poet.
I can't remember which one, but I always think of this.
Probably it's Issa who writes:
*The night is long.
The night is so long.
Buddha is great.*
Isn't that wonderful?
*The night is long.
The night is so long.
Buddha is great.
Buddha is great.*
And it is so wonderful that Buddha has so many voices.
Now, I haven't yet gotten around to my talk, but the last thing before I start is I have to tell you a word about my friend Kevin Killian, whom we did service for yesterday.
As I said, he died on Saturday.
He was famous, loved, a very important person in our wonderful San Francisco literary scene.
He was a really important member of that scene for many, many decades.
He grew up as a devout Catholic in New York, and he moved to San Francisco as a young man in the late 70s or so.
That was right in the middle of the raging and super exciting gay scene in San Francisco, which I think perhaps the world has seen nothing like ever before.
It was amazing.
And of course, even more amazing in another way when it became the AIDS epidemic.
Kevin was right in the thick of it.
He just kept doing things.
He was the founder of the famous Poets Theater in San Francisco, which will be forever famous in literary history.
He wrote and performed many plays in the Poets Theater.
He also founded Small Press Traffic, which is one of the premier arts venues still in San Francisco.

He was also an important member of a literary movement called The New Narrative, which did groundbreaking work, writing never before seen, ironic and absolutely outrageous gay erotic writing that would make you blush all over just to read the first page.
He was also the very, very careful scholarly editor of a volume called *My Vocabulary Did This to Me*, the collected poems of Jack Spicer.
Jack Spicer was also an important literary figure, long now past, of the San Francisco scene.
So Kevin was a bit of a historian, a literary historian and scholar also.
He was also a tremendous fan boy of all kinds of movies.
He was an expert on every kind of movie.
The worse the movie, the better.
And he loved celebrities.
He would run around looking for celebrities and trying to get their autographs all the time.
Somebody said that when Kevin once went to Colorado, he was dying to get someone to show him the house where JonBenet, that young girl, was murdered.
That was the kind of thing that he loved.
He really wanted to see the house.
He was also a great speller.
He actually won the New York City Spelling Bee when he was a kid.
It's hard to do, right?
The whole city-wide Spelling Bee.
Plus, every year the small press distribution would have a fundraiser that was a Spelling Bee, and Kevin would win it every single year.
They finally had to stop doing it because Kevin would always win it.
He also had the most wonderful marriage to his long-time partner, Doty Bellamy.
Wondrous and wonderful because Doty is more or less known as a gay woman, and Kevin was an unmistakably gay man.
So this was at first a head-scratching thing, but it was a most wonderful marriage.
They were happily married, beautifully married.
They loved each other deeply for many, many years.
They were actually the king and queen of the San Francisco literary life, although it was hard to tell sometimes which was the king and which was the queen.
Doty was in touch with me, and I was in touch with her wonderfully.
I'm glad I was at Kevin's deathbed.
I think I mentioned yesterday that somehow or other they got a Catholic priest to show up who chanted the litany of the saints, and they all chanted with him.
So I just wanted to tell you that, and I appreciate very much that you helped me remember Kevin, whom I will miss.
So I'm really happy that we're doing this.
This is the first time we're doing oryoki here at Samish, and I love oryoki practice.
We were just down at Tassajara for a 90-day ango period, and we did oryoki every day, and it's such a wonderful thing.
It's the greatest way for human beings to eat.
It's like a dance.
It's actually quite similar to tea ceremony, in which every single movement is precise and meant to be a thing of beauty.

It may seem to you ridiculously elaborate and way too complicated, but when you think about it, it is actually by far the most efficient way possible for 70 people to serve and eat a meal while simultaneously performing a religious ritual, practicing the maximum mindfulness, and washing and putting away the dishes, all in about 40 minutes.
This is really quite something.
You have to admire our Zen ancestors for having invented such a practice.
There are, to be sure, tremendous refinements and details possible, probably refinements and details that most of us are totally unaware even exist, let alone whether we're doing them or not.
I hope that as the week wears on, you will consider that you can learn and refine these details, because when you do them all, I can't tell you what a beautiful pleasure it is.

Usually, and the reason why we haven't done it all this time is because, it's sort of a rule of thumb that you can't do oryoki unless the sangha is preparing the food, because there are lots of specific guidelines and details about the food that you would never expect any food service to do.
It's just too much.
The serve-up is so complicated.

But here at Samish, Laura and her gang, our good friends, have been taking care of us for so long and with such loving kindness that I guess they kept stretching their generosity until the boundaries on the other side of the oryoki disappeared.
Yeah, and I hope that by the end of the week they will not regret it.
The same thing actually happened to us in the Bay Area, a very similar story.
We had people that were feeding us who loved us and we loved them dearly, and finally they did do oryoki and they did regret it.
Although they still seem to be doing it anyway, but they regret it.
Anyway, it's wonderful that we're doing this.
I thought this morning I would like to devote my words to talking about the chanting service that we do during the meal.
We're saying all this stuff when we eat, and I think in a way there's nothing mysterious about what we're saying.
It's all pretty clear, and the more you repeat it, I think the more you will understand it on your own.
But anyway, I thought I would say a little something about these words today, which we didn't make up.

They do come from the Chinese monastic code, maybe from the Song dynasty, and then were translated from Chinese monastic life, monastic practice, into Japanese, and then translated from Japanese into English, originally by Suzuki Roshi and some students of the Zen Center, but re-translated in the 1990s by a big official committee of Buddhist scholars and practitioners.
*Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, enlightened at Magadha, taught at Varanasi, entered nirvana at Kushinagara.
Now we set out Buddha's eating bowls.*
So we begin the meal by remembering Buddha's life, and these are the main events of Buddha's life: his birth, his awakening, his teaching, his nirvana.
And so we're like that too.
We're born, we get enlightened, we're teaching, we enter nirvana.
So that's life.
One, two, three, four, boom, over.
So life is quick.
Four things happen.
It's quick, but it's very important, and we do not forget a life, and we don't forget Buddha's life.
I think Buddha's life here is being proposed as the ideal human life, the basic template of a good human life.
To be born into this Saha world, which contains exactly the right amount of suffering.
To be born in this Saha world is to be given what you need to awaken.
And then of course, when you're awakened, you do what you can to help people and other sentient beings.
And then when you're done, you pass away, and you offer your body to the earth, and you make room for the next guy to come along and do the same.
This ideal life does not necessarily include your crazy destructiveness and your dark confusion.
Those things might be there as part of your path to awakening, but when you awaken, you put all that aside so that you can be maximally helpful to others.
Doing good for yourself and for others is a very good thing.
In a complicated world where it's quite hard to tell exactly what is going on or what one should do, this we can absolutely count on.
Doing good is good.
Being destructive and harmful to others and to the planet is not good.
That much, I think, is quite clear.
We also know from our experience that when we do good, we feel good about our life, and we're being of service.
And when you live like that, then when you enter nirvana, just like the Buddha, it's okay.
You can enter nirvana knowing you did your best.
Anyway, we remember all this, this model of a life we aspire to, when we begin our meal.
And we are imagining that as we're eating this meal, we are ourselves the Buddha.
And we're imagining, as we say, that these simple plastic or wooden or ceramic bowls are actually Buddha's bowls.
They're not our bowls that we got at the store or something.
They're Buddha's bowls.
In the monastic archetype, bowls are a big deal.
They say the grand design of robe and bowl: these physical objects define the Buddha's life.
If you ordain as a priest, you receive the robe and the bowls in the ceremony, and they are consecrated in the ceremony as Buddha's robes and Buddha's bowls.
They're not yours.
They never were.
They never will be.
And this is a serious thing.
We absolutely believe it.
These are Buddha's bowls.
So when we eat the meal, we pay attention with reverence to these bowls, and we take good care of them.
We eat out of them lovingly.
We wash them carefully.
We fold them up with awe, because they're not just regular stuff.
A lay person's bowls are actually the same, because there's no such thing as lay person's bowls, right?
Lay people don't eat out of bowls.
They eat out of regular tableware.
So if you're here in sesshin, eating out of bowls, these are also Buddha's bowls.
So that's the spirit.
And that's why we say that in the beginning, to set our hearts clear on what we're doing.
*Now we set out Buddha's bowls.
May we, with all beings, realize the emptiness of the three wheels: giver, receiver, and gift.*
So here we're setting an intention, which is another way of saying we're praying.
They say Buddhists don't pray, but actually we're praying in the meal chant.
Whenever we say "may we," that's a prayer, right?
So as we open up these bowls, we're not just salivating over the tasty food that we're about to eat, and we're hungry, and we can hardly wait to eat.
No, we're praying, wishing, desiring, intending to realize something that we've never realized before.
And we want to realize this not only for ourselves, but for and with everyone else.
And what we want to realize is the emptiness of the three wheels: giver, receiver, and gift.
This thought comes from the Diamond Sutra, one of the emptiness sutras, which is using Dhanaparamita, the practice of giving, as an example.
And it says, giving is empty.
There is no giving.
There's no such activity because there's no giver and no receiver and no gift, so there can't be any giving.
So the point is we're about to eat this food.
This food has been given to us as a gift, and so we want to use this gift to realize the emptiness of giver, receiver, and gift, and giving.
And it's true, as the meal chant will note a little later, that we didn't shop or cook or grow this food, and mostly we didn't cook it.
In a traditional monastery, the food is literally given to the monastery by the donors.
And here we, the sangha, are our own donors.
When we pay the cost of the meal of this session, we're donors.
So it's slightly different for us.
We're our own donors to ourselves, in a way, instead of someone else donating.
But still, the food is given, and we're grateful.
So point one is, notice, this is a gift, an offering.
Point two, there is no gift, no receiver, no giving.
And this is because these three wheels, the three wheels that turn the whole world, because the whole world is built on a foundation of generosity, these three wheels, this generosity is empty.
Oops.
I didn't get that.
Sorry, Siri.
I'm going to explain now.
I'm going to explain now.
She doesn't understand the emptiness of the three wheels.
Probably you don't either, so I'm going to explain that now.
Yeah, I'll explain now.
So what is this empty?
It's a head-scratcher, right?
What are we talking about?
And why would we aspire, of all things, to realize this emptiness, and wish that everyone else would also realize it?
Emptiness doesn't sound like that attractive a thing to be realizing.
So what is it all about?
Well, too long a story to go into.
I try, actually, my best to explain it in my book, The World Could Be Otherwise, so maybe some of you will read it, and you can tell me whether I do a good job explaining this.
But for now, let's just say this.
That things are empty is to say that things are not at all the way they seem.
They are already, in fact, otherwise.
They seem small.
They're very big.
They seem painful.
They're blissful.
Instead of bounded, they're without any boundary.
Emptiness is the real shape of the world.
Everything flowing together, everything cooperating all the time.
The world certainly does not look like that to us, but it really and truly is that way 100% of the time.
Even when we are painfully feeling it's otherwise, it is not the way we painfully think it is.
It really is a blissful, perfect world all the time.
Everything really is love.
This world wouldn't appear without generosity and love, and nothing other than love.
So this is why we really want to realize the emptiness of giver or receiver and gift, and this is why we want everyone to realize this.
And we say giver or receiver and gift, but it doesn't just mean giver or receiver and gift.
We say it because we're about to receive food, so that's why we say it in terms of giver or receiver and gift, but it means all the time, everything is empty.
And this is the point, not only of breakfast, lunch, and dinner, it's the point of our whole practice, of our whole lives.
All dharmas are empty, all dharmas are free, all dharmas are nothing but sharing and love all the time.
And this is what we are reminding ourselves of as we open up our bowls.
This is what we are praying for in eating this meal.
So we carefully, beautifully, set out our bowls.
It's a very precise way that the bowl should be set out on the tray, and the chopsticks and the spoon in a very precise way.
They're taken out of the case in a very specific way and placed in a specific way on our table.
When the bowls are set forth, the Kokyo will chant later, *this morning meal of ten benefits nourishes us in our practice.
Its rewards are boundless, filling us with ease and joy.* I'm saying this a little out of order; that comes after the invocation that I'm going to speak about in a minute.

*This food of ten benefits nourishes us in our practice, its rewards are boundless, filling us with ease and joy.* So there are ten benefits listed traditionally to our food, stuff like it's good for your complexion, it prevents you from having a stomach ache, we hope.
It maintains your strength and longevity, etc.
There's ten things like that.
But then it says, never mind those ten, its rewards are boundless, more than just ten.
And this beneficial food fills us with ease and joy.
And I hope you feel this.
The meals, oryoki meals in sesshin, are particularly happy times.
I hope you're happy when you eat your oryoki meal.
It's a very happy thing to sit and eat.
It brings you ease and joy.
Delicious food.
You can eat your food and pay attention to your food and forget about all your problems and all the problems in the world.
They don't exist.
You're just eating this wonderful food.
In the afternoon, the Kokyo chants, *the three virtues and six tastes of this meal are offered to Buddha and Sangha.
May all sentient beings in the universe be equally nourished.* You don't offer food to Dharma, because Dharma doesn't eat anything, but Buddha and Sangha eat, so you offer it to Buddha and Sangha.
And the three virtues are softness, cleanness, and beautiful preparation, because the food is prepared not like ordinary food, but with a special loving heart.
And that is true in the kitchen here.
The food is prepared with spiritual attitude and effort.
Six tastes are sweet, spicy, salty, bitter, sour, and simplicity.
And the tenzo, the cook, is supposed to know these six tastes and balance them carefully.
In the morning, when we chant the verse, we're starting out the day, so we haven't eaten since a long time.
So we're concerned that we build up our strength to get through the day.
So that's why we emphasize in the morning chant the physical benefits of the food for strengthening us for the day.
But in the afternoon, by that time, we're already rolling along pretty good.
So now we're ready to notice a little bit more the delicate flavors of the food.
And we're ready to remember that we're not just eating for ourselves.
We're praying that as we eat, also may others eat, that no one will go hungry.
And we don't do it here because it's a little bit too complicated.
But in the monastery at lunch, we actually make an offering.
We take a little piece of our food from the first bowl, and we put it on the end of our setsu.
And the servers come around and collect that little piece of food from everybody, and they offer it to the spirits.
So then before these little solo chants by the chanter, we are chanting the invocation.
So an invocation is an amazing phenomenon, not so much known in our times of rational discourse.
An invocation is sort of like a magic, magical act.
By the magic of the voice and the words and the intention, you summon the presence of those creatures, those beings that you invoke.
So by saying the names of the great buddhas and bodhisattvas, who by definition do not exist, they are by definition imaginary.
They are not meant to be historical beings who lived and died and ate food.
We chant their names together in unison with a unified intention, and by this magical incantation, we actually bring them forth.
We bring them here.

We call these the ten names of Buddha, and we chant them any time we find ourselves in need of the help of these guiding spirits to consecrate something we're about to do, and we're always calling them forth any time precepts are offered, any time there's an ordination ceremony, we call forth the ten names of Buddha, because we understand that a regular person by herself, by himself, could not possibly give precepts or receive precepts.

In order to do that, you need Buddhas and bodhisattvas and deities and special imaginary beings to be present, so we invoke them, and this means that serving food is also a sacred ritual that requires this kind of assistance, because think about it.
Eating actually is a mysterious thing.
It is a kind of miracle.
You take carrots and mushrooms or oatmeal or whatever, and somehow or other you transform it into love, into wisdom, into human activity.
How did you do that?
You chew it up, you swallow it, and God only knows how this whole thing transpires.
Nobody really knows how does this happen?
Eating really is a sacred miracle, and so naturally we have to summon Buddhas and bodhisattvas to come and consecrate this act that we are preparing to accomplish.

So we call on *Vairocana Buddha, the Pure Dhammakaya, Locana Buddha, Complete Sambhogakaya, Shakyamuni Buddha, the Myriad Nirmanakaya,* and these three are the triple body or the three bodies of the Buddha.
The Dhammakaya is the Cosmic Buddha body, the Buddha beyond anything and everything.
They call it usually the Reality Body.
The Dhammakaya Buddha is maybe, we could say, the whole universe that exists and doesn't exist beyond the simple physical model of the universe that we would understand.

It's an esoteric Buddha, Vairocana Buddha, very important in tantric Buddhism, and although Soto Zen is not classified as a form of tantric Buddhism, in fact, our rituals are very much inspired by tantric Buddhism.
So we invoke Vairocana, the Dhammakaya Buddha.
We invoke Locana, the Sambhogakaya Buddha.
The Sambhogakaya body of Buddha is the enjoyment body of Buddha, the blissful body, sometimes called the bliss body of Buddha.
This is the Buddha of pure meditation bliss, a body without any defilements, perfect in every way.
This is the Buddha that we meet in the Mahayana Sutras, sitting on the lotus throne expounding the Dharma.
And also, once in a while, this Sambhogakaya Buddha is you.
When you enter the various trance states of meditation practice beyond the ordinary kamadhatu, when you enter the rupadhatu and the arupadhatu, you are coursing in the world of Sambhogakaya Buddha.
Shakyamuni Buddha, who looks like he lived and ate food and went to the toilet and died like any human, actually is the myriad Nirmanakaya Buddha, the manifestation body of Buddha.
And this body is myriad because it appears all the time everywhere in all world systems, but not cosmically, not beyond the physical world.
She or he appears only in particulars, as this or that particular person.
Maybe every blade of grass and every rock and tree is Shakyamuni Buddha, the myriad, endlessly appearing particular Nirmanakaya.
Then we chant the name of Maitreya Buddha, a future birth, the Maitreya Buddha, the Buddha of the coming era.
Shakyamuni Buddha is the Buddha of this era.
We know Shakyamuni's story and we talk about it and so on, but we don't know yet the story of Maitreya Buddha because Maitreya Buddha hasn't come yet.
She or he is the Buddha of friendliness, the Buddha of loving kindness.
Maitreya means friendliness or kindness.
It's actually the same word as Metta.
We know the word Metta, but Maitreya is the same word in Sanskrit.
So I think we can all be cheered up to know that what is coming for this world, the next Buddha that is coming, is the Buddha of loving kindness and friendliness.
Although it might not look at this moment as if this is the way the world is trending, we don't really understand how causality works.
We only see as far as our eye can see.
We don't understand that actually this is coming, loving kindness, friendliness.
This is what we're moving toward in the future.
So this should cheer us all up.
Then, for good measure, in case we might have left somebody out, we just mention all buddhas throughout space and time.
That should cover it.
Then we mention the Lotus of the Wondrous Law, the Mahayana Sutra.
So oddly, we're mentioning here a sutra in this list of Buddhas.
Why would we do that?
Well, this Lotus of the Wondrous Law is somehow like such a marvelous sutra that it goes beyond being a sutra.
It's like a Buddha in itself, this sutra.
And you probably know that in some Buddhist schools, they just basically dispense with everything other than not only the Lotus Sutra, but you don't even need the Lotus Sutra.
All you need is the name of the Lotus Sutra.
Just chant the name of the Lotus Sutra, and that's all you need to do.
That's how powerful the Lotus Sutra is.
And in China, the Lotus Sutra was considered to be the supreme sutra.
It was the central sutra.
All sutras were realized and set in context by the Lotus Sutra.
And Dogen loved the Lotus Sutra.
So I think it was Dogen who added the Lotus Sutra to this list of the Ten Names of Buddha.
Then comes the three most important imaginary Bodhisattvas, Manjushri, who appears, as we have him over there on the left, as a youth brandishing a sword in one hand, a book in the other.
The book is the Prajnaparamita Sutra, the Sutra on Emptiness.
And the sword cuts through all complications and contradictions and delusions.
Only a youth brandishing a sword can do that.
Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva of activity or work practice, the Bodhisattva of doing.
And I can't ever think of Samantabhadra, Bodhisattva, without thinking of dear Blanche Hartman, our Dharma sister and co-abbot who loved Samantabhadra, always spoke of Samantabhadra.
And I have a Samantabhadra figure that Chris gave me.
Samantabhadra is always riding on an elephant.
That's how you can tell it's Samantabhadra.
Then, yes, that's right.
So you can take a look at Samantabhadra over there.
And then Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of love and compassion, Guanyin, Kannon.
She has 10 different forms.
Sometimes she has many hands and arms, heads and arms.
Sometimes she's holding a jug of water, spilling water to nourish a parched world.
So this is the great triumvirate of Bodhisattvas that we remember when we're about to eat our meal, because we always have to practice wisdom and action and compassion.

Again, next, for good measure, in case we left anyone out, we include all honored ones, all sages, all Bodhisattvas, mahasattvas, which I think includes not only all the Buddhist sages, but all the sages everywhere, in all religions and in non-religions, all the good beings of the universe who are of benefit.
We honor them all.
We bring them all to us.

And then at the very end, to put a cap on the ten Buddhas, we also honor Maha Prajnaparamita herself, wisdom beyond wisdom, who, as we chant in the morning, is conceived of as a great, gorgeous goddess, mother of all the Buddhas, source of all the Buddhas.
She herself is an organ of vision where she has a clear knowledge of the own being of all dharmas as empty.
And she never ever strays away from that vision.
So we summon these magical beings with our words, our hearts, to witness our meal.
Pretty soon it will be lunchtime.
So when we chant, see if you can feel.
Maybe they're behind you or around you.
I think really if you try, you can feel the presence of these bodhisattvas in the room during the meal.
After we serve and chant the single verse I mentioned before, when everybody's served, we chant the five reflections.
First, we remember that a lot of effort went into bringing this food to us.
I think literally it says something like, 72 labors brought us this food.
I think the way we translated it in our centers was, innumerable labors brought us this food.
Before we eat, we should remember with gratitude all that went into bringing us this food.
That's the first reflection.
The next reflection is we take a look at ourselves and we ask ourselves, wow, all the work that went into bringing this food to me, do I actually deserve this food?
Do I have enough virtue?
Is my practice strong enough and virtuous enough to deserve this food?
And the answer is no, it's not.
That's the correct answer.
I do not have sufficient virtue and practice to deserve this food.
Now, in our contemporary worldview, which is very serious, we don't look at it like that, because we have the idea of rights and entitlements.
Such ideas were absolutely unknown in ancient China.
Everything we received, they thought, we received as a gift.
We didn't earn it and we never really deserve it.
Now, this does not at all imply, as it would for us, that we are miserable sinners and terrible people and we should feel badly about ourselves.
We don't even deserve our lunch.
This is not the intention of saying this and feeling this.
The idea is we are humble and grateful to be alive.
We're happy that we're alive.
We didn't make this happen.
It happened to us and we are very grateful for it, and we know that it's not ours, it's given.
Thank you.
Ego itself, which is necessary, is by its nature arrogant, full of pride, prideful.
So we have to say this to remind ourselves that no, we don't want to live that way.
The third contemplation is the commitment not to be greedy.
We're going to eat.
Oryoki means just enough.
We're going to eat just enough food, as much as we need, as much as we desire, but no more.
And because of this commitment not to be greedy, we can really, really, really enjoy this delicious food.
Even if it's not delicious, it's delicious because of our commitment to non-greed.
Every morsel of food is absolutely delicious.

When we're eating, just to be eating, when we're eating with that simplicity, not eating to fill some kind of boundless empty hole inside of ourselves, not eating with the unconscious fear that someone's going to snatch away our food from us, or whatever other crazy ideas we're eating with all the time, no, we're just going to eat, period.

And then we note that this food sustains our life, and that's why we're eating, to continue to live, because we've been given this life, which is such a good thing, such a blessed thing, and we're going to take care of it.
We're going to use it well.
That's why we're eating.
And the last contemplation is to remember that we're eating for the sake of our practice, which is our life, which is our commitment to do good and be of benefit to others.
We're eating to continue the Buddha way.
So then we say, okay, now we've thought about all that, so now we're going to eat.

And just one last thing: before we start eating, we remind ourselves this is dedicated in thanks to the three treasures, Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and to the four benefactors, which include our parents, our various kinds of benefactors, including, shockingly enough, the government.
You didn't know that.
We didn't translate it.
We didn't lay it all out, but among the four benefactors is the government.
Yes, thank you, government, because there are no armies besieging Samish Island.
Thank you, government, for preventing armies from invading us.
Thank you, government, for making the roads that got us here.
Thank you for preventing chaos and crime.
The government ensures our safety and protects us.

In ancient China, at the time when these verses were written, it was absolutely automatic that you had faith in the emperor and the government for the protection and the stability that it offered you.
In fact, I believe that in China today, people still appreciate the government for that same reason.
And by and large, they support the government, though they are not stupid and they're aware of the many serious ways in which the government is oppressive.
But I think that most people in China today prefer this oppression, though it is far from ideal, to the chaos and social unrest that they have known in the past.
Now, our liberal Western view is actually quite different from this.

Whether we know it or not, we actually all have a sort of Christian utopian view that government should not only ensure stability and protection, but much more importantly than that, it should ensure justice and well-being and freedom and full inclusion for everyone, which is why we are generally disappointed in our government, because it has so far not done any of those things.
So we actually have quite high expectations of our government.

And that is a good thing, because if we continue to have high expectations, perhaps one day in the future the government will fulfill these expectations, and let's constantly work for a government that will.
But also we should recognize that this is a little over the top.
Such expectations, particularly when you realize all the governments in history, right?
The sum total of them, how often have governments delivered this?
Well, I can tell you, never.
And there have been some today, now, and in the past, pretty terrible governments.
And then before there were any governments, I think it was probably worse.
So let's keep our high expectations, but perhaps it helps to think of them in the context of a broader history.
Anyway, we're dedicating the merit of our meal ceremony to the three treasures, the four benefactors, and finally, for good measure, to everyone else, everywhere in all the six realms.
Not only all the human realm inhabitants, but also the inhabitants of the hell realms, the fighting demon realms, the animal realms, the hungry ghost realms, all the realms.
And then we bow to the three bowls and we get ready to eat.
And we imagine each of the bowls, one, two, and three, being one of the three pure precepts: to do no harm, to do good, and to save all beings.
And just before we take the first bite, we pray that we will realize the Buddha way.
So we did all of that stuff.
And then we eat.

And then when we're done eating, we chant a little verse that also, as a magic, magically transforms this ordinary, perhaps slightly by now yucky water into ambrosia for the various spirits to whom we will offer it.

So when we collect this water, we should consider it to be very special water that has been consecrated by all the Buddhas that we have summoned, by all our prayers and good intentions that we have imbued into this water that we're now returning to the spirits from which it came.
And then we say:
*Oh, maha kushalaya, maha kushalaya, svaha.*
So earlier I mentioned the committee that was translating this.
I was on that committee.
And I remember when we translated this little part, we got into an argument.
Phil Whalen said, this refers to a weird Chinese deity.
And Reb Anderson said, no, no, it refers to great goodness.
Maha kushalaya means great wholesomeness.
And Philip said, no, that is too whitewashed.
It's a deity, a demon.
It's even a demon, and we're invoking this horrible demon to protect us.
So we got into a big argument and Reb won the argument.
It actually doesn't say in Chinese maha kushalaya at all.
It actually says the name of this demon.
But it's likely they're both right in a way, because probably the name of the demon comes from the word maha kushalaya.
And the Chinese turned it into a demon because Chinese Buddhism is full of demons and folklore and all this.
It's quite extraordinary, and most of it we've sanitized from our discourse.
We also had an argument, a worse argument, a more important argument, over the last chant of the meal, when the Kokyo chants.
We used to chant:
*May we exist in muddy water with [unclear: "purity of water"], with purity like a lotus.
Thus we bow to Buddha.*
And now, this was retranslated, and now it says:
*Abiding in this ephemeral world like a lotus in muddy water, the mind is pure and goes beyond.
Thus we bow to Buddha.*
We didn't like that way at all.
We liked the first way much better.
And we had a big argument about this because we didn't want to say the mind is pure and goes beyond.
We didn't want to think our practice was about purification and going beyond the muddy water of the world.
It seemed so dualistic to us.
It seemed like that wasn't our practice at all.
We were very attached to the idea that the lotus grows in muddy water, which is true.
The lotus does grow in muddy water.
If you go to India and you drive along the road where the fields are, there are all these ditches full of muddy, icky water.
Do not drink that water along the fields.
And lotuses do grow in those ditches.
So they do grow in muddy water.
However, it is also true that the lotus flower comes out of that muddy water and stretches above the water.
It's not the flower itself in the water.
So the plant is in the water, but the flower goes beyond.
And I remember Griff Falk, bless his heart, a scholar and translator from the Chinese.
We all ganged up on him, but he would not relent.
He said, no, it just doesn't say that.
It says exactly what I'm translating.
He gave up a lot of other battles, but he would not give in.
So now we're going beyond and the mind is pure from now on, from then on.
And actually, if you ever practice Chan, the source tradition of our Japanese Zen and of Vietnamese Zen and Korean Zen, you will see that there's a lot more dualistic talk.
There's a lot more emphasis on purification and overcoming vexations and all of that.
Our practice, as filtered through our dear Dogen, is quite different in that regard, at least the way we talk and understand is different.
Sorry, I went on far longer than I should have.
And I meant to, at some point, tell you to relax and change your legs so you're not dying there from sitting without moving.
But anyway, I'm done.
I did want to talk about the meal chant.
I think I seldom have done this, so that you can appreciate more each meal.
And of course, at dinner time, which is not a meal, it's officially not a meal, we don't chant, because we're not actually eating.
It's not really a meal.
So anyway, they are intentionally extend

verbatim.text: Well, you can all hear okay? Well, before I say anything, I just want to first off remember Nancy, dear Nancy Welch. Nancy, along with John Wiley. John's still here, right? practicing the maximum mindfulness and washing and putting away the dishes all in about 40 minutes. Yeah, and I hope that by the end of the week they will not regret. The same thing actually happened to us in the Bay Area, a very similar story. We had

people that were feeding us who loved us and we loved them dearly, and finally they did do oryoki and they did regret it. Although they still seem to be doing it anyway, but they regret it. It's all pretty clear, and the more you repeat it, I think the more you will understand it on your own. But anyway, I thought I would say

a little something about these words today, which we didn't make up. Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, enlightened at Magadha, taught at Varanasi, entered nirvana at Kushinagara. Now we set out Buddha's eating bowls. So we begin the meal by remembering Buddha's life, and these are the main events of Buddha's life. His birth, his awakening,

Those things that might be there as part of your path to awakening, but when you awaken, you put all that aside so that you can be maximally helpful to others. Doing good for yourself and for others is a very good thing. In a complicated world where it's quite hard to tell exactly what is going on or what one should do, this we can absolutely count on. Doing good is good. Being destructive and harmful to others and

to the planet is not good. That, I think, that much is quite clear. We also know from our experience that when we do good, we feel good about our life, and we're being of service. And when you live like that, then when you enter nirvana, just like the Buddha, it's okay. You can enter nirvana knowing you did your best. Anyway, we remember all this. This model of a life we aspire to when we begin our meal. And we are imagining that as we're eating this meal, we are ourselves the Buddha. And we're imagining, as we say, that these simple plastic or wooden or ceramic bowls are actually Buddha's bowls. They're not our bowls that we got at the store or something.

And if you ordain as a priest, you receive the robe and the bowls in the ceremony, and they are consecrated in the ceremony as Buddha's robes and Buddha's bowls. They're not yours. They never were. is you. Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva of activity or work practice, the Bodhisattva of doing. that Chris gave me. Samantabhadra is always riding on an elephant. That's how you can tell it's Samantabhadra. Then, yes, that's right, that's right, that's right.
